statements.text: General Nakasone. One of the things that this committee and the broader Congress has done is to create programs like Scholarships for Service that has been tremendously helpful for organizations like U.S. Cyber Command, but broader organizations within our government. [...] Artificial intelligence, machine learning, as many, as any members have looked at and talked about, is the future for our Nation, it is the future for our economy, it is the future for our national defense. So, any type of scholarship that would, obviously, focus young people on this growing importance of this field, where they are able to study it and then perhaps give back to any part of the government, I think is something that is honorable.
statements.context: House Armed Services Committee hearing on cyberspace operations, where Mr. Khanna asked General Nakasone about STEM scholarship ideas for AI and quantum fields.

statements.text: I believe that a lot of the work being done there on AI, on quantum, on advanced cyber is going to be critical for our national security, to prevent jamming of any of our communication systems, to be able to accurately identify and target. [...] Could you help explain from your perspective, from a Navy perspective, what we can do to adopt the latest technology and why that is going to matter for our future national security?
statements.context: House Armed Services Committee hearing on the FY2024 NDAA, with Rep. Khanna questioning Secretary of the Navy Del Toro about adopting emerging technologies for defense.

statements.text: I guess I'm trying to understand, what is the best data that is needed for AI to be effective in military applications? And does China have an advantage on that kind of data or not?
statements.context: Congressional hearing on AI in military applications, Representative Khanna questioning expert witnesses.

statements.text: China is spending almost 10 times as much as the U.S. as a percent of their military budget on AI, and we really need to think about the modern technologies that are going to be needed to have a most effective national security strategy.
statements.context: Opening remarks by Rep. Khanna at a House Armed Services Committee hearing on AI in military applications.

statements.text: Maybe I will quickly ask my last question, which is, do you think we need any DOD clearance for any types of AI like we have for nuclear technology? There are safeguards. There is only so many people who can get access to it. Mr. Wang, is there anything analogous in the AI space?
statements.context: Congressional hearing titled 'Man and Machine: Artificial Intelligence on the Battlefield,' with a lawmaker posing a final question to a witness.

statements.text: he said that AGI [artificial general intelligence] was 5 to 6 years away. I was surprised by that timeline. What is your sense of how long we are from AGI?
statements.context: Representative Ro Khanna poses a question during a House hearing on AI on the battlefield.

statements.text: My concern is it will just be terrible. You know, they are not going to produce Hamlet. It will just be the further devolution of entertainment.
statements.context: House hearing on federal agency use of AI.

statements.text: And one of the concerns I have is that there is been an overhyping of AI as a form of human intelligence, which I just think is giving our species less credit than we deserve.
statements.context: Rep. Ro Khanna speaking during a House Oversight Subcommittee hearing on federal AI use.

statements.text: Could you talk about what it would mean for our national security and our ability to have a lead in AI if we just started defunding MIT [Massachusetts Institute of Technology], University of Pennsylvania, Harvard, and many of these universities?
statements.context: House hearing on DOD technology and AI operations, Rep. Khanna questioning Dr. Martell.

statements.text: Third, let us make sure that these private insurance companies can't rely on AI to have AI-generated algorithms that deny claims. No AI used to deny Americans' claims.
statements.context: Representative Khanna delivers a one-minute floor speech advocating for Medicare for All and interim insurance reforms.

statements.text: How would you address people's concerns about AI displacing jobs, being something that will lead to layoffs or people not being able to work?
statements.context: Rep. Ro Khanna poses a question to a panel during a hearing on the federal government in the age of artificial intelligence.

statements.text: One of the things I am most concerned about is the jobs situation. Now, obviously AI is going to create a lot of new jobs, but you look at college unemployment today. [...] and there are projections that that will increase as entry-level jobs, in particular, are affected.
statements.context: Rep. Ro Khanna poses a question about AI and employment at a hearing or event titled "Algorithms and Authoritarians: Why U.S. AI Must Lead."

statements.text: I wonder whether you think that, for certain high-risk AI applications, there should be some minimum threshold of mandatory third-party verification, even if that third party verification is just verifying the company's own standards HZS176000                                 PAGE or some threshold that we need to move towards.
statements.context: Representative Ro Khanna questions an Anthropic executive at a congressional hearing on U.S. AI leadership.

statements.text: And who would design those tests? Is it the AI Institute, or is it the private sector? Who comes up with what those tests should be?
statements.context: Congressional hearing titled 'Algorithms and Authoritarians: Why U.S. AI Must Lead,' with Rep. Ro Khanna questioning a witness about AI testing oversight.

statements.text: So in this case, I mean, I have articulated a need for AI safety regulations to protect Americans, to protect consumers, to protect jobs. But would it be fair to say that we need smart regulations for our own national security, that having AI regulation and a strong, robust agency is needed for national security? I will let the witnesses answer and then my time is up.
statements.context: Congressional hearing on China's theft of U.S. AI technology, during a Q&A with witnesses.

statements.text: Do all of the witnesses think that the distillation is the biggest security threat to the United States right now in terms of China getting AI models?
statements.context: Rep. Ro Khanna questions witnesses at a congressional hearing on China's efforts to obtain American AI technology.

statements.text: And would all of you recommend that this AI institute at Commerce be beefed up in terms of the safety regulations and security regulations?
statements.context: Rep. Ro Khanna questions expert panelists at a House hearing on China's campaign to steal America's AI edge.
